text: Gilles de Rais, Baron de Rais (also spelled Retz; c. 1405 – 26 October 1440), was a French knight and lord from Brittany, Anjou, and Poitou, a prominent leader in the French army during the Hundred Years' War, and a companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc. He is primarily known for his conviction on charges of the rape and murder of several children. As a major noble heir to influential feudal families, including the House of Craon through his mother and the Laval family through his father—one of the two most important Breton lineages in the 15th century—he rallied to King Charles VII of France and fought against the English. In 1429, he formed an alliance with Georges de La Trémoille, the Grand Chamberlain of France, and was appointed Marshal of France that same year following successful campaigns with Joan of Arc. Little is known about his personal relationship with her, unlike the fictionalized portrayals in literature. He gradually withdrew from military action during the 1430s. His family accused him of mismanaging his wealth by selling off lands to fund his extravagant spending, leading to an interdict by Charles VII in July 1435. In May 1440, he assaulted a high-ranking cleric at the church of Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte, seized the local castle, and violated ecclesiastical immunity, undermining the authority of Duke John V of Brittany. Arrested on 15 September 1440, he was tried in October 1440 by an ecclesiastical court assisted by the Inquisition for heresy, sodomy, and the murder of "one hundred and forty or more children," and simultaneously condemned by secular judges of the ducal court for his assault and crimes against "several small children." On 26 October 1440, he was executed by hanging and burning at the stake alongside two of his servants. A popular confusion between Gilles de Rais and the mythical Bluebeard has existed since the early 19th century, despite the uncertain claim that he may have inspired Charles Perrault's fairy tale "Bluebeard" (1697). In the late 19th century, his case has often been interpreted as a serial killer case, though this categorization is sometimes considered anachronistic. Most historians believe he was guilty, but some caution against interpreting the trial records without considering historical context. Medievalists Jacques Chiffoleau and Claude Gauvard emphasize the need to analyze the inquisitorial process, particularly the influence of judicial expectations on confessions, and the role of rumor in shaping Gilles de Rais's public reputation (fama publica), without ignoring testimonies about missing children or confessions describing unusual rituals. Gilles de Rais, son of Marie de Craon and Guy de Laval-Rais, was born in a room called the Black Tower at Champtocé castle at an unknown date, with birth dates variably cited between 1396 and 1406, more often toward the end of 1404; however, he was likely born not before 1405 due to legal delays in his parents' marriage, according to archivist-paleographer Matei Cazacu, whose view is accepted by several medievalists. An archival document notes Gilles's age as "14 to 15 years old" in February 1422. His younger brother René was probably born in 1414. Gilles obtained the seigneury of La Suze from his elder brother on 25 January 1434, before the ducal court in Nantes, after which René was known as René de La Suze. Marie de Craon died at an unknown date, and her husband Guy de Laval-Rais died at the end of October 1415 in Machecoul, suffering from a serious bodily infirmity, though the cause of death remains unknown—some authors incorrectly claim he was disembowelled by a wild boar during a hunting accident, a fictional scene from a 1928 French novel. The two orphaned brothers were raised by their maternal grandfather, Jean de Craon, lord of La Suze and Champtocé. Jean de Craon's son Amaury died at the Battle of Agincourt in October 1415, prompting Jean de Craon to take control of the property of Gilles and René, thus overriding the will of Guy de Laval-Rais, which had appointed Jean II Tournemine de la Hunaudaye as guardian. On 4 January 1417, Jean de Craon betrothed his grandson Gilles to Jeanne Paynel, daughter of Foulques VI Paynel, but the Parlement of Paris blocked the marriage until Jeanne came of age; the union never occurred, though Jeanne later became an abbess of Lisieux. Jean de Craon then betrothed Gilles to Béatrice of Rohan, daughter of Alain IX of Rohan and Marguerite of Brittany, with a contract dated 28 November 1418, which was not pursued for an unknown reason (possibly due to Beatrice's death). Gilles eventually became engaged to his third cousin Catherine de Thouars, daughter of Miles II de Thouars and Béatrice de Montjean. Despite being fourth-degree relatives, disputes arose between the Craon and Thouars families. Ignoring consanguinity and without seeking ecclesiastical dispensation, Gilles abducted Catherine and married her in a chapel outside his parish, without publishing banns. Their marriage was annulled and declared incestuous by the Church. After Miles II de Thouars died, matrimonial alliances helped reconcile the Craon and Thouars families. On 24 April 1422, the papal legate asked Hardouin de Bueil, bishop of Angers, to sentence Gilles and Catherine to separation and impose penance before allowing them to marry properly. After an investigation, Hardouin celebrated their marriage with ceremony on 26 June 1422 at Chalonnes-sur-Loire, strengthening Gilles's position in Poitou by linking him to the Viscounts of Thouars, who dominated the Bas-Poitou region. Their only child, Marie, was born in 1433 or 1434. Under Catherine's marriage contract, her mother Béatrice de Montjean retained dower rights to Tiffauges and Pouzauges castles. Jean de Craon and Gilles hoped to recover these properties later, but when Béatrice remarried Jacques Meschin de la Roche-Aireault, a chamberlain to King Charles VII, their plans were thwarted. They commissioned their acolyte Jean de la Noe, captain of Tiffauges, to kidnap Béatrice and her younger sister, imprisoning Béatrice at Le Loroux-Bottereau and then at Champtocé. Gilles de Rais and Jean de Craon threatened to sew Béatrice up in sackcloth and throw her into a river if she did not surrender her dower. To free her and her sister, Jacques Meschin summoned Jean de Craon and Gilles before the Parlement of Paris, to no effect. He sent a bailiff and his brother Gilles Meschin to represent him, who were jailed by Jean de Craon. Eventually, Jean de Craon released Béatrice at the request of his wife Anne de Sillé, who was also Béatrice's mother. The other hostages were released on ransom, but Gilles Meschin died a few days later, likely from exhaustion. Jacques Meschin's younger sister was sent to Brittany and forced to marry Girard de la Noe, son of the captain of Tiffauges. Jacques Meschin then took legal action before the Parlement of Paris, leading to a compromise with Jean de Craon and Gilles. In a transaction ratified by the Parliament, Jacques kept Pouzauges, while Gilles retained Tiffauges. However, Jean de Craon and Gilles extorted Pouzauges on the grounds that Catherine de Thouars bore the name of Pouzauges. On his way to supervise the transfer, Adam de Cambrai, First President of the Parlement of Paris, was robbed by men acting on behalf of the two. Subsequent legal penalties against Jean de Craon and Gilles were ignored. As holder of the barony of Retz, traditionally one of the six oldest baronies of the Duchy of Brittany, Gilles de Rais was one of the most important lords of western France, owing to his extensive estates across Brittany, Anjou, Poitou, Maine, and Angoumois. Medievalist Philippe Contamine notes that Gilles was "Breton, Poitevin and Angevin all at once, due to his fiefs," and historian Georges Peyronnet highlights that his network of family and feudal relatives covered large parts of the western marchlands, which were difficult to access due to the damp climate and the Marais breton. The strategic position of the barony of Retz, at the southernmost point of the Duchy, encompassed a vast group of forty parishes between the Loire and the borders of Poitou and Brittany. Gilles held Machecoul (the "head of the barony"), as well as the castellanies of Coutumier, Bourgneuf, Prigny, and half of the Isle of Bouin, bordering the Bay of Bourgneuf. Salt marshes in the Bay likely provided significant revenue. He also held an annuity on the Paimpont forest and owned the townhouse "Hôtel de La Suze" in Nantes and the lordship of La Bénate, encompassing 26 parishes (13 in Brittany and 13 in Poitou). In Anjou, he inherited Champtocé and Ingrandes, a source of income from Loire trade, as well as Blaison, Chemellier, Briollay, Fontaine-Milon, Grez, and Grattecuisse. In Poitou, he held Cheneché, de la Voûte, Sigon, Cloué, Chabanais, Breuil-Mingot, and acquired by marriage and extortion the baronies of Pouzauges and Tiffauges. In Maine, he owned La Suze, Ambrières, Saint-Aubin-Fosse-Louvain, and Précigné. In Angoumois, he held Confolens, Loubert, and Château Morant. This list reflects Gilles's peak prosperity after marrying Catherine de Thouars in 1422 and following the death of his grandfather Jean de Craon in 1432. However, his estate diminished over time due to disposals, inheritances going to his brother René in 1434, and other transfers. His estates were not always valuable due to irrevocable alienations to vassals or the Church, widows' dower rights, declining saltworks in the Bay of Bourgneuf, and war-related damages requiring defensive expenditures. Several factors must be considered to explain his financial difficulties beyond mere mismanagement. Accurately estimating his wealth remains difficult due to fragmented or imprecise records, especially regarding estate yields. Historians Jacques Heers and Matei Cazacu disagree: Heers minimizes Gilles's wealth and social status, denying him the title of "great lord" and calling claims of him being one of France's richest lords "a figure of speech," while Cazacu disputes this, affirming Gilles's status as a powerful, wealthy, and sumptuous lord, citing a legal document from his heirs around 1461–1462 that attributed to him an annual income of 50,000 livres tournois—about 30,000 from estates and nearly 20,000 from his office as Marshal of France. While below the incomes of contemporary princes like the Dukes of Orleans, Burgundy, and Berry, this income placed Gilles in a high tier, accessible only to a small number of 15th-century Breton lords. Regardless of the estimate, his fortune was insufficient to sustain his lavish lifestyle over a few years. In the decades following the Breton War of Succession (1341–1364), the defeated faction continued to resist relinquishing its claim to the Duchy of Brittany and plotted against the Montfort dukes. A legal document drawn up by Gilles de Rais's heirs around 1461–1462 attributes to him an annual income of 50,000 livres tournois, with approximately 30,000 coming from his estates and nearly 20,000 from his office as Marshal of France. Although this income is below that of contemporary princes such as the Dukes of Orleans, Burgundy, and Berry, it still places Gilles de Rais in a high financial bracket, accessible only to a small number of 15th-century Breton lords. His wealth, however, proved insufficient to sustain his opulent lifestyle over just a few years. Following the Breton War of Succession (1341–1364), the defeated Penthièvre faction, led by Marguerite de Clisson and her sons Olivier and John, captured Duke John V in February 1420 in violation of the Treaty of Guérande (1365), gaining temporary support from Charles, Dauphin of France and future King. In response, the Breton nobility rallied to the House of Montfort under Duchess Joan, including Jean de Craon, who swore allegiance to her and John V on 17 February 1420. In retaliation, Penthièvre forces attacked Jean de Craon and his grandson Gilles de Rais, notably destroying the castle of La Mothe-Achard. After John V’s release, Jean de Craon and Gilles de Rais were rewarded with generous land grants converted into monetary gifts. While it is debated whether young Gilles participated in the final conflicts of the Breton War of Succession due to lack of documentary evidence, it is possible he entered the patronage of Arthur de Richemont, John V’s younger brother. During this period, France faced political and military setbacks due to the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War and conflicts with the Lancastrian monarchy. King Henry V of England secured his position as heir to Charles VI through the Treaty of Troyes in May 1420, and John V later aligned with the Treaty of Troyes in June 1422. Upon Charles VII’s ascension in October 1422, he continued the war against the English. Jean de Craon and Gilles de Rais may have participated in the victories at La Gravelle (26 September 1423) and Verneuil (17 August 1424), though this remains speculative. The defeat at Verneuil marked a significant military setback, completing the disaster of Agincourt nearly a decade earlier. Charles VII then sought allies, turning to Yolande of Aragon, head of the House of Valois-Anjou, who had been working since 1423 to strengthen ties between France and Brittany through her vassal Jean de Craon, Gilles de Rais’s grandfather. Jean de Craon, a wealthy Angevin lord with estates in Maine, Anjou, and Brittany, began gaining influence at the ducal court of Anjou from 1423–1424. In March 1425, Arthur de Richemont was appointed Constable of France, and in October 1425, Gilles de Rais appeared in the entourage of Charles VII during festivities sealing the Franco-Breton alliance in Saumur. In the same month, Charles VII asked Arthur de Richemont to return Breton lands to Gilles de Rais, specifically former estates of Miles de Thouars, father of Gilles de Rais’s wife. After the Maine conquest (1424–1425), the House of Lancaster threatened Anjou’s borders, with John, Duke of Bedford, claiming the region. The estates of the houses of Laval and Craon were exposed to English raids, and Arthur de Richemont suffered a crushing defeat at the Battle of St. James in 1426; Gilles de Rais’s presence at this battle is not confirmed. It is unlikely that Gilles de Rais and future judge Jean de Malestroit would have hated each other due to this event. Georges de La Trémoille became Grand Chamberlain of France in June 1427 and soon gained dominance in the Royal Council, creating a rivalry with Arthur de Richemont. On 19 June 1427, Yolande of Aragon appointed Jean de Craon lieutenant general in Anjou and Maine, a move coinciding with La Trémoille’s rise. As a distant cousin of Gilles de Rais, La Trémoille was also a member of the Craon family. Jean de Craon likely appointed his grandson Gilles de Rais’s military mentor, Guillaume de la Jumellière, lord of Martigné-Briant, a trusted advisor to Yolande. This familial influence led to Gilles de Rais’s appointment as captain of Sablé on behalf of Duke Louis III of Anjou. John V of Brittany, under English pressure, negotiated with John of Lancaster in July 1427 and shifted allegiance to the House of Lancaster, recognizing the Treaty of Troyes and ordering his vassals to cease fighting the English. Gilles de Rais, along with Viscount Alain de Rohan, Bishop Guillaume de Montfort, and Laval relatives, was one of the most prominent Breton lords to disobey his suzerain and remain loyal to Charles VII. Arthur de Richemont fell from favor due to the failure of the French–Breton alliance, despite retaining the title of Constable, and left the court to engage in conflict with La Trémoille without joining the English. From mid-1427, chronicles begin to mention Gilles de Rais alongside other French captains, leading guerrilla warfare on the borders of Maine with Ambroise de Loré and his relative Jacques de Dinan, lord of Beaumanoir. These raids enabled French forces to storm the Ramefort fortress at Gennes, where Gilles de Rais and others spared the English garrison but hanged the French-speaking men, possibly reflecting strong national sentiment against those seen as "disowned French" or supporters of the dual monarchy. In another operation, the lords of Rais, Loré, and Beaumanoir retook the castle of Malicorne from the English, executing the French-speaking besieged as at Ramefort. At the Battle of Château du Lude, Gilles de Rais killed or captured English captain Blackburn, according to conflicting sources. The exact chronology of these events is unclear due to medieval chronicle inconsistencies. In spring 1428, Gilles de Rais contributed a thousand gold écus to the ransom of his cousin André de Lohéac, captured by the English on 16 March 1428 during the siege of Laval. The House of Laval promised to reimburse the "very dear and beloved cousins and great friends" who assisted in the rescue. In June 1428, new English troops landed and laid siege to Orléans from October. In February 1429, Joan of Arc arrived in Chinon to speak with Charles VII, and Gilles de Rais was present at the Château de Chinon. A month later, on 8 April 1429, Gilles de Rais formed an alliance with Grand Chamberlain Georges de La Trémoille, pursuing a strategy of bilateral alliances to consolidate his position and protect against plots by Arthur de Richemont. Gilles de Rais sat on the Royal Council from 1429 to 1434, though infrequently, due to military duties or other reasons; his title may have been honorary, and he is also referred to as Charles VII’s chamberlain. As part of a Franco-Breton diplomatic rapprochement, likely supported by La Trémoille, Gilles de Rais wrote to John V in April 1429 urging him to reinforce the army assembling in Blois to aid Orléans. Meanwhile, Joan of Arc received authorization to join the relief army after being interrogated by French theologians in Chinon and Poitiers. On 25 April 1429, the Maid arrived in Blois to find a convoy of supplies and an escort of men-at-arms and archers commanded by Gilles de Rais and Jean de Brosse, marshal of Boussac, including a company of Angevin and Manceaux soldiers paid by Gilles de Rais, who appears to be central to this operation. Gilles de Rais contributed to lifting the siege of Orléans by participating in the storming of the Saint-Loup bastille on 6 May. He then took part in the Loire Campaign (1429), including the Battle of Jargeau on 12 June and the Battle of Patay on 18 June. On the way to Reims, Gilles de Rais and Jean de Brosse commanded the vanguard of the French army. On 17 July 1429, during the coronation, Gilles de Rais and three other lords carried the Holy Ampulla from Saint-Remi to the Metropolitan Church. On the same day, he was elevated to the rank of Marshal of France, either for his war record or due to political support from La Trémoille. On 15 August 1429, Charles VII entrusted the wings of his army to Jean de Boussac and Gilles de Rais at Montépilloy. On 8 September 1429, during the siege of Paris, Joan of Arc requested Gilles de Rais and Raoul de Gaucourt to be with her during the assault on the Porte Saint-Honoré. Gilles de Rais stood by her all day, attempting to cross the Parisian wall from a rear ditch, and at nightfall, Joan was wounded in the leg by a crossbow bolt. The siege was lifted, and the coronation army withdrew to the Loire and was dismissed at Gien on 21 September 1429. That month, Charles VII reaffirmed Gilles de Rais’s title of Marshal and granted him the right to add a border bearing the fleur-de-lis to his coat of arms, a royal favor shared only with Joan of Arc. On an unspecified date, a military expedition led by Xaintrailles and La Hire settled in Louviers, seven leagues (about 28 kilometers) from Rouen, where Joan of Arc was imprisoned since 23 December 1430. Gilles de Rais is attested in Louviers on 26 December 1430, and some historians interpret the troop movements as an attempt to free Joan of Arc, though this is unproven and no such delivery occurred. In parallel with his campaign against Anglo-Burgundians, Georges de La Trémoille continued his "private war" against Arthur de Richemont, supported by the House of Valois-Anjou. Gilles de Rais supported La Trémoille, his cousin and ally. Despite similar policies toward Brittany and Burgundy, La Trémoille eventually became a "repellent" by uniting various factions at the court, paradoxically strengthening the Angevins. The young Charles of Anjou, future leader of the Royal Council, joined the governing body on 30 March 1430 through his mother Yolande of Aragon. On 26 October 1430, Charles of Anjou appointed Jean de Bueil captain of the garrison at Sablé, a post previously held by Gilles de Rais and royal governor Jacques de Dinan, lord of Beaumanoir. Civil war broke out again in September 1431 when La Trémoille.

The policies pursued by the House of Valois-Anjou and La Trémoille regarding the Duchy of Brittany and the Burgundian State led La Trémoille to gradually act as a "repellent" by uniting various factions against Charles VII, paradoxically strengthening the Angevins at the French court, according to medievalist Laurent Vissière. The young Charles of Anjou, future head of the Royal Council, joined this body on 30 March 1430 through his mother, Yolande of Aragon. On 26 October 1430, as king's lieutenant general in Anjou and Maine, Charles of Anjou appointed Jean de Bueil captain of the men-at-arms and archers garrisoning Sablé, a post previously held by Gilles de Rais and royal governor Jacques de Dinan, lord of Beaumanoir. In September 1431, La Trémoille sent Captain Rodrigo de Villandrando into Anjou, which led to a civil war; in 1432, Jean de Bueil defeated the Spanish mercenary, though the latter later ravaged Bueil's Touraine lands. According to Le Jouvencel's romanticized account, Gilles de Rais imprisoned Bueil in Sablé (referred to as "Crathor"), but Bueil escaped and regained the town, only for Gilles de Rais to recapture it in a night attack. On an unknown date, the garrison of Champtocé attacked Yolande of Aragon en route to Brittany, where Gilles de Rais and Jean de Craon's men stripped her convoy of horses and baggage. In August 1432, Gilles de Rais helped lift the siege of Lagny, alongside the lifting of Orléans, through a "double movement of troops" involving Rodrigo de Villandrando crossing the Marne upstream before La Ferté-sous-Jouarre and French forces entering through a weak point, causing the English to abandon their positions. Medievalist Françoise Michaud-Fréjaville notes this as a major feat, though she references Jean Chartier's "not always very reliable" account. Chartier also mentions Gilles de Sillé, cousin of Gilles de Rais, among the troops after the siege, possibly confusing him with Michel de Sillé, another relative; during Gilles de Rais's trial, the families of missing children and the accused's confessions cast suspicion on Gilles de Sillé, who was on the run, and a rumor, attributed to Michel de Sillé's servants, claimed the English demanded twenty-four young hostages as ransom, a claim deemed "absurd" and "implausible" by Noël Valois and Olivier Bouzy. Jean de Craon, Gilles's grandfather, died in November 1432, and Gilles de Rais inherited his estates and castles, including the Hôtel de La Suze in Nantes and Belle-Poigne in Angers, likely organizing his patrimony in 1433 with his wife Catherine de Thouars, during which their daughter Marie was born. In June 1433, a plot against Georges de la Trémoille was uncovered in Chinon, leading to his removal; at the Estates General in Tours in September 1433, Charles VII confirmed his fall, restoring Valois-Anjou's influence, making Charles of Anjou the key figure in the Royal Council, and granting "great government and authority" to former allies of La Trémoille, including Jean de Bueil and Gilles de Rais. Gilbert Motier de La Fayette regained his marshal title after losing it to Gilles de Rais in 1429, likely due to La Trémoille's actions. In February 1434, the English threatened Sillé, the fief of Anne de Sillé, widow of Jean de Craon; the House of Laval (Guy XIV de Laval and André de Lohéac) and Gilles de Rais participated in a military expedition under Constable Arthur de Richemont, with Gilles de Rais commanding the vanguard alongside Pierre de Rieux and others, though he appeared isolated among lords aligned with La Trémoille's enemies. The armies arrived before Sillé but separated without fighting. By mid-1434, despite being absent from court, La Trémoille urged Gilles de Rais to continue fighting the Burgundians, but Gilles, likely ruined by expenses, made little effort to prevent Philip the Good's capture of Grancey in August 1434; Charles VII then summoned Gilles and threatened to strip him of his marshalship, with Philippe Contamine suggesting he was likely replaced by André de Laval-Lohéac. On 2 July 1435, Charles VII placed Gilles de Rais under interdict due to complaints from his brother René de La Suze and the House of Laval. Most information about Gilles de Rais's financial mismanagement comes from a 70-folio brief written around 1461–1462 by his heirs, an expanded version of the 1435 interdict document. Not all medievalists trust this source; Jacques Heers considers it too incriminating, while Philippe Contamine calls it both "tendentious and instructive," and Matei Cazacu regards it as "the most important document known to date on Gilles de Rais ... a formidable effort to reconstitute the discrepancies of a life and a personality." Accounting records on Gilles de Rais's expenses and estate management are incomplete, making it difficult to verify claims of prodigality; for example, the 1430s-minute register of notary Jean de Recouin, covering Gilles's stay in Orléans from September 1434 to August 1435, is damaged, with the first and last pages unreadable and many pages cut or missing since the 19th century. The heirs accused Gilles de Rais of "insane expenses" from age 20, including maintaining a troop of two hundred mounted men, though this point is not emphasized, possibly due to heirs' caution in criticizing military spending, which was vital given the royal treasury's low funds and Gilles's proven role in supplying Orléans in April 1429. The first sales of Gilles's estates occurred during his early campaigns; in 1429, he sold Blaison for 5,000 écus to Guillaume de la Jumellière, lord of Martigné-Briant, a transaction that angered Jean de Craon. Between 1434 and 1435, after being disgraced by Charles VII, Gilles de Rais withdrew from public and military life. Testimony from priest Eustache Blanchet and cleric François Prelati indicates Gilles sent Blanchet to find alchemists; Blanchet recruited Prelati in 1438 during a trip to Florence. Prelati claimed to have attempted to summon a demon named "Barron" at Tiffauges in Gilles's presence and interrogated him in a meadow near Josselin, close to where Duke John V of Brittany met Gilles on 14 July 1440. Gilles provided a contract with the demon for riches to be given later; after three failed summonings, Gilles grew frustrated, and Prelati stated Barron demanded child parts, which Gilles offered in a glass vessel, but without success, leaving him bitter and financially ruined. In his confession, Gilles de Rais admitted to his first assaults on children between spring 1432 and spring 1433. After entrusting Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte to René de La Suze in 1434, Gilles reclaimed it by force and later reached a deal with his younger brother in Nantes on 15 January 1439. He then sold it to Geoffroy Le Ferron, treasurer of Duke John V, who transferred its administration to his brother Jean Le Ferron, a high-ranking cleric; Gilles attempted to reclaim it and sell it to his cousin, the Sire de Vieillevigne, but Jean Le Ferron resisted. In retaliation, on Pentecost or the day after (15 or 16 May 1440), Gilles ambushed a troop of fifty to sixty men in a wood near Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte, entered the parish church, interrupted the mass of Jean Le Ferron, insulted him, and threatened to kill him with a guisarme if he left; the cleric fled with Marquis Lenano de Ceva, opened the castle gates, and was imprisoned. Gilles also arrested or roughed up other ducal agents, such as Jean Rousseau. This action simultaneously violated divine and ducal authority: by committing sacrilege and targeting ducal servants, all within the diocese of Bishop Jean de Malestroit, the influential chancellor of Brittany ("the man actually responsible for the duchy's political direction," per Joël Cornette). John V ordered Gilles to return the stronghold to Jean Le Ferron, imposing a fine of 50,000 gold écus; Gilles then transferred his prisoners to Tiffauges, a fortress outside Brittany's jurisdiction in Poitou. In July 1440, Gilles went to Josselin to meet Duke John V, though the discussions remain unknown; according to Prelati's later confession, Gilles sought to secure his freedom before meeting the duke and asked his Italian invoker to summon "Barron" in a meadow near Josselin to question the demon about John V's intentions. Shortly after the attack on Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte, an ecclesiastical investigation (inquisitio infamiae) was launched. The process began with gathering testimony on the accused's reputation (fama) within a legal framework; Bishop Jean de Malestroit visited Nantes, starting at the parish of Notre-Dame, Gilles's residence, to investigate rumors of missing children. On 29 July 1440, the Bishop issued letters patent accusing Gilles de Rais of raping and murdering children, demonic invocations, and pacts. Simultaneously, secular authorities, under Jean de Touscheronde for Pierre de L'Hôpital, the universal Judge of Brittany, heard the same witnesses. On 24 August 1440, Duke John V met with his brother Arthur de Richemont, Constable of France, in Vannes to secure mutual aid after being compromised in the Praguerie in spring 1440; as part of this, John V granted Richemont the land of Bourgneuf-en-Retz, owned by Gilles de Rais. Richemont then returned to France and seized Tiffauges, freeing Jean Le Ferron. Gilles de Rais was summoned to appear before the ecclesiastical court of Nantes on charges of "murdering children, sodomy, invoking demons, offending the Divine Majesty and heresy." Two days later, on 15 September 1440, he was arrested at his Machecoul castle by Jean Labbé, a captain in arms for the Duke of Brittany. Among the accused were François Prelati, Eustache Blanchet, servants Henriet Griart and Étienne Corillaut ("Poitou"), and Tiphaine Branchu and Perrine Martin ("la Meffraye"), accused of being child providers. Gilles de Sillé and Roger de Briqueville, likely already on the run, were not apprehended. Gilles de Rais was imprisoned in the Château.

John V granted his brother the land of Bourgneuf-en-Retz, which was owned by Gilles de Rais. Richemont then returned to crown lands in France and seized Tiffauges, freeing the hostage Jean Le Ferron. Gilles de Rais was summoned before the ecclesiastical court of Nantes on charges of "murdering children, sodomy, invoking demons, offending the Divine Majesty and heresy." Two days later, on 15 September 1440, he was arrested at his Machecoul castle by Jean Labbé, a captain in arms serving the Duke of Brittany. Among the accused were cleric François Prelati, priest Eustache Blanchet, servants Henriet Griart and Étienne Corillaut, known as "Poitou," and Tiphaine Branchu and Perrine Martin, known as "la Meffraye," two women accused of being child providers. Gilles de Sillé and Roger de Briqueville, likely already on the run, were not apprehended. Gilles de Rais was imprisoned in the Château des ducs de Bretagne in Nantes. He was prosecuted in both secular and ecclesiastical courts on charges including murder, sodomy, and heresy. The extensive witness testimony convinced the judges of sufficient grounds for guilt. After Gilles de Rais admitted to the charges on 21 October, the court cancelled a plan to torture him. Peasants from neighboring villages had earlier accused their children of entering Gilles de Rais's castle to beg for food and then disappearing. On 23 October 1440, the secular court heard the confessions of Poitou and Henriet and condemned both to death, followed by Gilles de Rais's death sentence on 25 October. The ecclesiastical court imputed to him the murders of "one hundred and forty children, or more," while the secular court mentioned only "several small children" as victims. Gilles de Rais was allowed to make a confession, and his request to be buried in the church of the monastery of Notre-Dame des Carmes in Nantes was granted. Execution by hanging and burning was set for Wednesday, 26 October. At nine o'clock, Gilles de Rais and his two accomplices proceeded to the place of execution on the Ile de Biesse. Gilles de Rais is said to have addressed the crowd with contrite piety, exhorting Henriet and Poitou to die bravely and think only of salvation. His request to be the first to die had been granted the day before. At eleven o'clock, the brush at the platform was set afire and Gilles de Rais was hanged; his body was cut down before being consumed by the flames and claimed by "four ladies of high rank" for burial. Henriet and Poitou were executed similarly, with their bodies reduced to ashes and then scattered. In his 1756 work Essai sur les mœurs et l'esprit des nations, Voltaire briefly referred to Gilles de Rais as a supplicant accused of magic and of slitting children's throats to use their blood for alleged enchantments, expressing reservations about his guilt but avoiding a definitive stance, using the trial to criticize "fanaticism composed of superstition and ignorance" as a flaw of the medieval period. In a 1784 passage from L'art de vérifier les dates des faits historiques, Benedictines from the Congregation of Saint Maur seemed to agree with Voltaire, asserting that Gilles de Rais "disgraced himself in Brittany by infamous deeds" but then suggesting that the "horrors" imputed to him may have been "of which he was perhaps not guilty," attributing them to "alleged soothsayers and magicians." Between 1902 and 1912, Salomon Reinach, a French archaeologist and historian of religion, proclaimed Gilles de Rais's innocence, a thesis developed in a context involving debates on religion, the Dreyfus Affair, and the scientific spirit, and criticized by Noël Valois in 1912. In 1921, French poet and writer Fernand Fleuret, following Reinach, defended Gilles de Rais's innocence with an anti-clerical interpretation, adopting the pseudonym "Dr. Ludovico Hernandez" to lend scientific credibility. In 1930, during the "Forbidden Conference" in Oxford, Aleister Crowley argued for Gilles de Rais's innocence, portraying him as a victim of the Catholic Church and describing him as "in almost every respect ... the male equivalent of Joan of Arc," whose crime was "the pursuit of knowledge." Margaret Murray, in her book The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, speculated that Gilles de Rais was a witch and adherent of a fertility cult centered on the pagan goddess Diana. Most historians reject Murray's theory; Norman Cohn argues it is inconsistent with known facts about Gilles de Rais's crimes and trial, and historians do not regard him as a martyr to a pre-Christian religion, instead viewing him as a lapsed Catholic who descended into crime and depravity, with his real crimes coinciding with land forfeitures. In 1959, Georges Bataille co-edited with Pierre Klossowski a modern French translation of the 1440 trial proceedings, including an introduction and lengthy appendix retracing Gilles de Rais's life. Bataille argued that Gilles de Rais's sexual crimes are "indubitable" because 15th-century judges could not have devised such a complex and perverse plot, and that understanding such behavior required later works by Marquis de Sade and Sigmund Freud, which "explore these abysses" and "force humanity to recognize their existence." Bercé notes that Bataille's approach may have been linked to a "personal exorcism" related to his own obsession with transgression and horror, explaining his belief in Gilles de Rais's guilt as a way to "cope with the vertigo that the twentieth century gave him." In 1992, French poet and novelist Gilbert Prouteau published a book imagining a modern re-trial of Gilles de Rais, including narrative texts, excerpts from minutes, romanticized letters, and a fictitious diary presented as that of an alchemical scholar, alcoholic, and aesthete apologist for pedophilia. Prouteau organized several publicity events, including an unofficial mock trial in November 1992 at the Clemenceau Hall in the Luxembourg Palace, where an informal "Court of Arbitration" composed of lawyers, writers, former French ministers, parliament members, a biologist, and a medical doctor, before Judge Henri Juramy, found Gilles de Rais not guilty. Commenters noted inaccuracies, as no participants sought professional advice from qualified medievalists. Medievalist Michel Balard criticized the rehabilitation promoters for seeking "the sensational, the pathetic, the sulphurous" rather than scientific history, and for lacking respect for documents and historical limits. Jean Kerhervé noted Prouteau's lack of research into primary sources and challenged his knowledge of religion, law, and medieval institutions in Brittany. Olivier Bouzy pointed out errors and biased inventions deliberately forged for rehabilitation. Archivist-paleographer Matei Cazacu criticized the syllogism used to exonerate Gilles de Rais ("The Inquisition persecuted the innocent. One of Gilles de Rais's judges was an inquisitor. So Gilles de Rais was the innocent victim of the Inquisition") as resembling the logician in Eugène Ionesco's play Rhinoceros. Journalist Gilbert Philippe of Ouest-France declared Prouteau "facetious and provocative," claiming he thought the retrial was "a monumental farce" pulled off with "high-ranking buddies." The "vast majority" of historians believe in the truth of Gilles de Rais's crimes, including medievalists Olivier Bouzy, Jacques Heers, Matei Cazacu, and Valérie Toureille, who find it impossible to "bank on the innocence" of Gilles de Rais despite the material interests of John V, Duke of Brittany, and his chancellor Jean de Malestroit, Bishop of Nantes. Claude Gauvard emphasizes that historians do not accept the conspiracy theory that the trials were orchestrated by Malestroit and the Duke of Brittany, noting that the initial witness accounts make the abduction of male children no mere rumor, and that facts are "stubborn things." Chiffoleau notes that the confessions of Gilles de Rais and his servants are not accurate shorthand but after-the-fact reconstructions based on the medieval inquisitorial system of pre-determined questions, notarial transcription, and torture to produce confessions that often merely confirm prosecution claims. Chiffoleau insists he is not proving guilt or innocence but explaining the weight of the proceedings and the judges' strong views on lese-majesty offenses, which in the Breton magistrates' eyes constituted a triptych of rebellion against the divine order, dealings with the Devil, and "unnatural relations" such as sodomy. Claude Gauvard argues that confessions were shaped by judicial expectations and the "fear of a demonological epidemic" during the witch hunts, making it "difficult, if not impossible" to distinguish fantasy from reality in the descriptions. Chiffoleau is puzzled by vivid passages in Étienne Corillaut's confession of 17 October 1440 describing bloody and orgasmic rituals, which have no precedent in other inquisitorial interrogations, as such details had not been recorded before Marquis de Sade's 18th-century works. No description or portrait of Gilles de Rais from his lifetime has survived; all depictions are posthumous and imaginary. According to Bataille and Klossowski's translation of the "confession in judgment" in the Latin acts, Gilles de Rais declared he had "always been of a delicate nature" during his youth. Michel Hérubel interprets this as physical complexion, but Matei Cazacu notes the adjective delicatus can also mean "cute, sought-after, luxurious, effeminate, gallant, licentious." The first description of Gilles de Rais—"a man of good understanding, good looks and good manners"—appeared late in a 1582 book, Histoire de Bretaigne, by Breton jurist Bertrand d'Argentré. Essayist Michel Meurger notes that this work first gave the judicial Gilles de Rais a body and mind, marking the beginning of a historical interplay across centuries. In 1841, Jules Michelet devoted four pages to Gilles de Rais in the fifth volume of Histoire de France, quoting fully the apocryphal description by d'Argentré without naming him, referring instead to vague tradition, thus popularizing the image of Gilles de Rais as an intelligent nobleman with handsome features: "He was, it is said, a lord 'of good understanding, good looks and good manners.'" In 1863, Auguste Vallet de Viriville added imaginary details: "He was a handsome young man, graceful, petulant, with a lively, playful spirit, but weak and frivolous." In the 19th century, medical science contributed to the "reification" of the ultra-romantic legend of Gilles de Rais as an alleged "superior degenerate," magnified by Joris-Karl Huysmans in his novel Là-bas (1891) as a Faustian scholar, artist, flamboyant mystic, and "great sadist." In contrast, Georges Bataille portrayed him as a "sacred monster" whom "war has accustomed to the voluptuousness of blood," an archaic, infantile, and stupid feudal lord without moral restraint, driven by a "monstrous Herostratus complex." Between 1870 and around 1900, sexual psychopathology developed significantly in Europe, with studies classifying all forms of "sexual perversions," and the most influential work being Richard von Krafft-Ebing's Psychopathia Sexualis (1886), which included a chapter on sexual sadism and invoked Gilles de Rais, greatly influencing later publications. Toward the end of the 19th century, these inventories of cruelties, obsessions, and perversions contributed to a renewed perception of recidivism.

Between 1870 and around 1900, sexual psychopathology developed significantly in Europe, with numerous studies aiming to classify all forms—both benign and criminal—of "sexual perversions." Medievalist Zrinka Stahuljak notes that preoccupations with criminality, criminal responsibility, and penal law revealed connections between madness and crime. The most influential work of this period was Richard von Krafft-Ebing’s *Psychopathia Sexualis* (1886), which included a chapter on sexual sadism that referenced Gilles de Rais, profoundly influencing later publications about him. By the end of the 19th century, inventories of cruelties, manic obsessions, and perversions helped shape a renewed understanding of recidivism and led to the emergence of the term "serial killer." In 1899, French criminologist Alexandre Lacassagne distinguished various types of sadists in his book *Vacher l'éventreur et les crimes sadiques*, identifying "great sadists" who committed "repeated crimes," including Gilles de Rais, Jack the Ripper, and Joseph Vacher. This shift replaced the image of the 15th-century heretic and rebel with that of the sadistic criminal, consistent with the scientific and journalistic frameworks of the time. Gilles de Rais, thus, became part of the "monsters" depicted in judicial chronicles such as *Le Petit Journal* and *La Gazette des tribunaux*. Physicians and historians of health sought to establish medicine as a key element in historical understanding through famous cases; Gilles de Rais was portrayed as a "criminal degenerate," symbolizing the alleged moral decay of the French medieval nobility—believed to have been corrupted by "vice" introduced during Norman incursions and the Crusades—within the outdated medico-moral frameworks of the late 19th century. This categorization reflected the French medico-legal school’s belief in the possibility of "physical and moral regeneration" via public hygiene and eugenics, with Gilles de Rais and Joan of Arc being retrospectively seen as the figures of depraved noble crime and popular genius, respectively, illustrating the theory of degeneration, which mirrored fin de siècle anxieties about societal decline. Historian Angus McLaren criticized the medical literature as often scientifically unsound, noting that Gilles de Rais and Antoine Léger were frequently grouped with other sadists and sexual murderers in fetishistic compilations of clinical cases. The original judicial records from 1440 remained largely inaccessible due to slow publication and fear of scandal, so physicians in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on Paul Lacroix’s *Curiosités de l'histoire de France* (1858), a fictionalized account of the trials. At the time, physicians believed they had found the cause of Gilles de Rais’s sadism in his reading of Tacitus and Suetonius, which described decadent Roman emperors’ orgiastic excesses; however, no evidence confirms these authors were in his library. Zrinka Stahuljak argues that "fiction facilitated Gilles' passage from historical to medical discourse," as Lacroix’s narrative provided a "scientific explanation" of his behavior. Three medical dissertations on Gilles de Rais were published between 1910 and 1934, described by Jacques Chiffoleau as "thin and disappointing," heavily influenced by Paul Lacroix and Joris-Karl Huysmans. In 1910, Dr. Augustin Cabanès used the pseudonym "Rondelet" to discuss Gilles de Rais’s facial tics and bluish beard—details derived from Lacroix’s fiction. In 1921, Fernand Fleuret posed as "Dr. Ludovico Hernandez" to publish an essay on Gilles de Rais. Chiffoleau observes that the limited erudition and frequent use of pseudonyms suggest these works were less scientific and more aimed at appealing to collectors of "curiosa" filled with sex and blood. More recently, psychiatrists Marie-Laure Susini, clinical psychologist Nicolas Brémaud, and Canadian cultural studies professor James Penney have examined Gilles de Rais using psychoanalytic approaches. Chiffoleau acknowledges their analytical potential but criticizes their "overly literal reading" of trial records, which overlooks the role of inquisitorial procedures in shaping the documents, and their reliance on the fictionalized narratives of Eugène Bossard, Georges Bataille, or Paul Lacroix. The connection between Gilles de Rais and the serial killer category was sometimes used to argue against his innocence, citing figures like Fritz Haarmann. In contemporary discourse, Gilles de Rais is sometimes viewed as an archetype of a dangerous media figure, described by Anne-Claude Ambroise-Rendu as "the pedophile conflated with the rapist-murderer — a reimagined Gilles de Rais, embodying both the predator and the madman." Didier Lett defines Gilles de Rais as a "sadistic child sex offender, sodomite, and serial murderer," while archivist-paleographer Matei Cazacu identifies traits in him consistent with modern serial killers and applies the FBI profiler’s "reading grid" and Michel Bénézech’s classification. Cazacu acknowledges the anachronism of this approach, stating that modern techniques should not be neglected, though he admits his method is contested and that the "abysses of the human psyche remain unfathomable" and that Gilles de Rais has kept his secrets. Claude Gauvard emphasizes that historians are not psychoanalysts, even if psychoanalysis helps interpret confessions and psychotic delirium. Jacques Chiffoleau maintains that the psychology of Gilles de Rais is forever closed to us, asserting that from the meagre evidence, we cannot determine whether he was a serial killer. He notes that the idea of an "almost timeless perverse structure" is only "distantly related" to the medieval accusations of rebellion, pact with the Devil, and unnatural relations. Although Gilles de Rais’s confessions appear to reflect a mixture of psychosis and narcissistic perversion typical of modern serial killers, his story offers little insight into pedophilia or serial murder in the Late Middle Ages. Sociologist and criminologist Aurélien Dyjak argues that projecting the modern "serial killer" category onto historical figures risks erasing their historical context, trajectories, and motives, creating a reductive and inadequate framework that fosters the illusion of historical continuity and turns the serial killer into a "criminological catch-all," reinforcing the idea that such crimes are timeless and universal. Gilles de Rais may have influenced Charles Perrault’s "Bluebeard" (1697), though this connection is disputed as too fragile. Since then, Bluebeard has been frequently conflated with Gilles de Rais in travel reports, oral traditions, and tourist activities, despite significant differences between the two. According to Matei Cazacu, this confusion stems from the difficulty of transmitting memories of child sexual abuse, and Bluebeard has become entwined with the memory of castle ruins in western France—former estates of Gilles de Rais—helping to anchor the tales in a tangible, physical space. The duality between Joan of Arc and Gilles de Rais is a common theme in fiction, but 15th-century archives do not establish a special relationship between them. Joan of Arc’s feelings toward Gilles de Rais are entirely absent from historical records, and there is no evidence that he withdrew to his lands after her burning at Rouen, becoming depressed and murderous; instead, her death may have been a "narcissistic" rather than "sentimental" rupture, ending an epic that fulfilled his ambitions for glory. A link between the Louviers expedition and a possible liberation attempt of the Maid is plausible but not confirmed. In 1439, Orléans acquired a banner from Gilles de Rais for a celebration of the lifting of the English siege, though it is not certain he supported the Mystery of the Siege of Orléans. In the same year, Gilles de Rais appointed Jean de Siquenville, a squire from Gascony, as commander of troops to take Le Mans, a force previously led by Jeanne des Armoises, a Joan of Arc impersonator; however, the relationship between Jeanne and Gilles de Rais remains "poorly documented and difficult to interpret."
